newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan FTC survey backs Fuji Photo in film dispute.
newsitem.headline: Japan FTC survey backs Fuji Photo in film dispute.

text.p: Japan's Fair Trade Commission (FTC) said on Wednesday that it could not find any business practices by Fuji Photo Film Co Ltd which violate the nation's anti-monopoly rules in the domestic film market.

In its survey of makers, distributers and wholesalers of photo film, the fair trade watchdog said it could not find any examples of Fuji Photo forcing shops to carry its products exclusively. Fuji Photo dominates the photo market in Japan.
Fuji Photo said on Wednesday that it welcomed the report, saying it appreciated "the detailed and thorough effort" by the FTC.
Japan's Trade Ministry said in a statement that the survey was proof of its position that imported film and paper are not blocked from distribution in Japan.
But the United States called the survey a "whitewash" of what it said were unfair distribution problems in the industry.
The FTC survey also called for weak and woefully insufficient recommendations for addressing anti-competitive practices, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said in a statement.

Fuji Photo and its biggest rival Eastman Kodak Co have been locked in a long-running dispute over access to Japan's photographic film market, which the U.S. government has said is a trade spat between two countries and not a fight between the two firms.
The FTC's report said the vast majority of Japanese retailers, including photo speciality shops and large stores, carry Kodak film, or have a source from which they are able to obtain Kodak film.
The report also said that Fuji's business practices do not violate Japan's Anti-Monopoly Law.
"Fuji Photo has always respected the voluntary decisions of the wholesalers, and will continue to respect them," the company said in a statement.
Barshefsky's statement said the FTC also failed to take serious enforcement action to fully eliminate the unfair practices.
"The survey findings whitewash the significant distribution problems that exist in this sector," she said.

Earlier this year, the United States filed a complaint with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) alleging that for the last 30 years Japan has imposed laws, regulations and other administrative steps to strengthen its domestic industry and curtail opportunities for foreign firms. The WTO is not expected to reach a decision on the dispute until October.
The FTC said Fuji Photo enjoyed over 70 percent of the market for colour film in Japan in 1995, when Kodak had a market share of less than 20 percent.

The FTC added that although any fresh entry into Japan's photo film market would be difficult because of costs and high-tech skills required, existing film makers have good opportunities to distribute their products through domestic retailers.

The fact some shops "...at present virtually sell only Fuji products does not immediately cause a problem in light of the nation's anti-monopoly laws," the FTC said, but it added that in terms of spurring competition, it was important to ensure the shops have the freedom to deal with any brand.

But the FTC said Fuji Photo should refrain from passing on complaints it receives from retailers about discount prices of its products to wholesalers, an action which the body said could hamper price competition in the market.
